entry.title: Champions of Krynn - A classic Gold Box RPG is reversed and bug fixed for the Amiga
entry.content:
Classic RPG fans running upgraded Amiga setups might have another reason to revisit Krynn this week thanks to a newly released reverse-engineered effort from developer mOoNsHaDo. Driven by a childhood love for SSI's classic Gold Box titles, mOoNsHaDo set out to make the Amiga port of Champions of Krynn play nicely with Kickstart 3.x, faster processors, and newer chipsets. Best of all, the updated executable now multitasks properly in the background alongside your regular Workbench apps, bringing a feeling of modernization to an incredible classic. 

The update squashes several nasty bugs that previously plagued expanded machines—even when running through WHDLoad. The patch resolves a blitter race condition on faster CPUs that used to leave bitplanes half-drawn and mess up LBM image colors, alongside an IPrefs screenmode promotion fix that stops mismatched monitor views from causing severe stretching or black screen flashing. It also clears up black flashing glitches tied to missing save games and patches out-of-bounds memory reads that caused random crashes. While this is available to download right now, mOoNsHaDo is asking players to send their save files over to marranosoft@gmail.com if they encounter bugs.

entry.title: Underworld Revisited - An open-source Unity reimplementation of Ultima Underworld 1 and 2!
entry.content:
If you love a bit of dungeon-crawling, then this latest update is for you! As PQMarine’s has teased their latest project, Underworld Revisited. Built in Unity as an open-source reimplementation of both Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss and Ultima Underworld 2: Labyrinth of Worlds, the engine bypasses DOSBox entirely by reading data directly from existing GOG, Steam, or EA app installations. The original title is playable from character creation to the final credits, faithfully executing original bytecode for everything from dialogue to trading while maintaining two-way save compatibility with the classic DOS version. 

While purists can play with authentic Palette lighting and fixes for game-breaking 1992 bugs, optional enhancements add widescreen support, modern mouse-look and gamepad controls, a live map, and a Remastered lighting mode featuring relief, shadows, and glow. You can also customise the audio with AdLib, General MIDI, emulated MT-32, or custom recordings, alongside full support for Underworld Editor (Avalonia) mods and a community translation kit. Behind the scenes, the project represents a massive revival over a decade in the making. PQMarine originally started the endeavour back in 2011 before putting it on hold in 2012, only picking it back up this September with the help of Claude Code—an AI-assisted workflow where Claude generates the code while the developer directs the features and tests everything step-by-step against the original source. Work on the sequel, Ultima Underworld 2, is already far along and available to test as an early preview, with only the cutscenes, ending sequence, and a full playthrough remaining before it reaches official beta status.

entry.title: Underworld Exhumed - A decompile of both incredible RPG DOS games with native ports for Windows and more!
entry.content:
Well here's another reason to visit this classic RPG series, as we welcome the latest update of Underworld Exhumed, a massive preservation project by developer abedegno that brings the 1992 classic Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss and its 1993 sequel, Labyrinth of Worlds, into the modern era. By reverse-engineering the original DOS executables, the creator has reconstructed the full source code for both titles. Not only has the code been cleaned up with readable names, shared headers, and helpful documentation explaining how each file works, but it is so accurate that compiling it with the original Borland tools produces byte-for-byte identical versions of the shipped UW.EXE and UW2.EXE files.

Abedegno has used this reconstructed code to build native ports for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing players to run both dungeon crawlers in a window complete with their original speech, music, and sound effects. Every tweak made to these ports is strictly verified against recorded DOS gameplay sessions to ensure total authenticity, though players will need to supply their own game data—such as the GOG releases—since the repository doesn't host copyrighted assets. For anyone who just wants to jump straight in without tinkering with files, the developer also compiled the port to WebAssembly, hosting a separate browser-based version that lets you explore both worlds with zero installation required.

Thanks @PixelCNinja for the heads up!

entry.title: Eddy & Co - A colourful DOS platformer from 1995 gets an Amiga port via mc68060
entry.content:
With Christmas fast approaching there's no wonder we'd start to see some festive like games appearing, and here we are with mc68060's latest DOS to Amiga 1200 port of Eddy & Co, a vibrant platformer that originally arrived on DOS back in 1995 as a free promotional title for Eismann. Rather than cutting corners for modern setups, this conversion aims for pure mid-nineties authenticity by arriving on a single floppy-disk image complete with a classic trackloader—capturing the exact feel of an official release from the era. Paired with crisp snowy visuals and a standout soundtrack from legendary composer Chris Huelsbeck, it is an ideal pick for a cold afternoon.

Once you load up the disk, you take control of Eddy and his three companions as they trek across a sprawling, frozen landscape. Players run and jump through four massive stages packed with icy hazards, snowdrifts, and stormy rain clouds while fending off a quirky roster of enemies ranging from rats and bats to polar bears and werewolves. Along the way, you can boost your high score by gathering sweets, top up your health with ice crystals, and snag cakes that let you hurl snowballs at incoming threats. Surviving each stage requires taking down a final boss to unlock the exit and push deeper into the winter wonderland.

  • Amiga 1200 or 4000 (AGA chipset), Kickstart 3.0 or higher
  • An unexpanded A1200 with 2 MB chip RAM is enough

entry.title: Krakout – Amiga AGA Enhanced Edition released by thall72!
entry.content:
Back in the heyday of the Commodore 64, Gremlin Graphics flipped the classic brick-breaker formula on its side—literally—with Krakout, a fast-paced arcade hit set to a memorable SID soundtrack by Ben Daglish. Despite its popularity, the game never received a dedicated Amiga 1200 release, a gap that developer thall72 has finally filled with Krakout Amiga AGA Enhanced Edition. Built entirely from scratch in native Amiga machine code with the help of AI to run at full speed on a stock 68020 processor without emulation, this release keeps the underlying gameplay logic completely faithful to the 8-bit original. Amiga gamers will find all 100 brick-filled screens, left-or-right bat placement, bonus bricks, and troublesome floating enemies intact, ensuring the frantic bounces feel just as they did decades ago.

While the core mechanics remain untouched, the audio visual presentation has been completely overhauled for the A1200’s AGA chipset. Players are greeted by a 256-colour hi-res intro showcasing the original cover art before diving into stages packed with shiny chrome-and-gold bricks, rich scrolling backgrounds, redrawn sprites, and a sleek new HUD. Daglish’s whimsical music has also been lovingly rearranged using sampled instruments and an added drum kit while preserving every original note and timing, backed up by crisp new sound effects for every smash and explosion. Rounding out the package are welcome extras, including high scores that save directly to disk and a streamlined options menu where a quick tap of the fire button toggles settings

Requirements

  • Amiga model: Amiga 1200 (or any AGA Amiga), stock, no expansions needed
  • Memory: 2 MB chip RAM, no fast RAM needed
  • Kickstart: 3.0 or 3.1
  • Video: PAL or NTSC, one disk works on both. On NTSC machines the game switches to 50 Hz so it runs at its original speed, which needs a display that accepts a 50 Hz signal; most RGB monitors and adapters do.
  • Media: ADF disk image (write-enable the disk to keep your high scores)
  • Tested on a real NTSC Amiga 1200 and in emulation

entry.title: Pole Position Remastered has been released for the Amiga & Atari ST by Jonathan Thomas
entry.content:
Here's a nice little treat for a Sunday, as we welcome the arrival of Pole Position Remastered, a brand new release for the Atari STE and Commodore Amiga (OCS/ECS/AGA). Created by developer Jonathan Thomas, the 2026 release is a complete, ground-up rebuild of his original 2017 STE port—which was crafted through manual reverse engineering—now overhauled using his deep knowledge of the hardware alongside AI assistance. By pulling the original arcade machine's exact game logic, graphics, and sound, the remaster delivers an almost authentic coin-op experience complete with real-time sprite scaling and a crisp 320x224 widescreen overscan display. While it is fully playable on standard 1MB machines, players with 2MB or 4MB memory expansions will benefit from even smoother performance.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Originally designed by Sho Osugi and released by Namco in 1982 as a follow-up to earlier electro-mechanical racers like F-1, Pole Position quickly became a global arcade phenomenon. Distributed in North America by Atari, Inc., the game claimed the title of Japan's highest-grossing arcade hit in its debut year before becoming the world's most popular coin-op title in 1983 (Wiki). Its dominance in North America continued as the top-earning arcade machine throughout 1983 and 1984—remaining in the top five well into 1985—making Thomas's faithful, enhanced 2026 port a fitting tribute to one of gaming's most influential racers.

entry.title: Space Harrier Enhanced - A classic game gets a 75% performance increase and other improvements on the Atari ST/STE!
entry.content:
Atari ST fans can finally experience a classic coin-op conversion the way it was meant to be played thanks to Space Harrier Enhanced, a newly released overhaul from developer Obsolete Media. The original 1988 ST port had its supporters, yet it suffered from sluggish frame rates and punishing difficulty that paled in comparison to the 1989 Commodore Amiga release. Set out to explore how a 1989 re-release utilizing the Blitter chip and Atari STe hardware might have stacked up against the Amiga, this edition pushes the engine to run 75% faster—jumping from the original's 8.81 FPS up to a much smoother 15.55 FPS—while slashing mouse latency from 124 ms down to 77 ms for far tighter controls. Alongside full-screen support, single-pixel background scrolling, faster loading times with a progress bar, and disk-saved high scores, STe owners get extra perks including higher-quality audio samples, smooth stage fades, and new colorful background modes inspired by the Amiga and modern reimagining's.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Gameplay has also been balanced to feel much fairer and closer to the arcade cabinet, introducing an optional two-hit energy system, arcade-style flashing boss weak points, an automatic attract mode, and a handy title menu to tweak lives, starting stages, screen sizes, and music. Perhaps most remarkable is how the project came together: built over roughly seven weeks between late September and mid-November 2026, Obsolete Media combined 70 hours of hands-on direction, benchmarking, and rigorous playtesting with 927 prompts fed into ChatGPT to overhaul the code. The result is a passionate technical showcase that gives the Atari classic a new lease of life.

entry.title: Enhanced framerate versions of Amiga games via AI and Vesuri - PART 2 (BIG FEATURE)
entry.content:
Using AI, Vesuri continues to update a large number of classic Amiga games, providing much-needed bug fixes and performance improvements As noted in our earlier coverage, Amiga enthusiasts have long dealt with a frustrating limitation: investing in high-end hardware upgrades—such as the famous Apollo 1240 accelerator card for the Amiga 1200—only to see older titles still suffer from sluggish performance. Because games from the early 1990s were rarely programmed to take advantage of faster, upgraded components, even top-tier setups failed to deliver smooth gameplay. Leaning on deep experience from the Amiga demoscene, Vesuri knew the hardware could do much better, fuelling a longtime goal to rewrite these underlying software bottlenecks and unlock the true potential of powerful accelerators.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Gunship Enhanced

For Gunship Enhanced, the game has seen a massive performance overhaul for accelerated Amigas. Pilots running 68020 or 68030 processors will notice drastically faster flight, achieved by shifting the stack and 3D models into fast memory, switching on the instruction cache, and letting the CPU handle polygons, sky, and lines instead of relying on the blitter—though CD32 owners will need an extra 1.2 MB of fast memory to handle the upgrade. Best of all, toggling the new enhanced framerate option (enabled by default in the installed icon via CUSTOM2=1) breaks the original 10.7 frames-per-second cap, letting the game run smoothly at its own natural pace and pushing performance to between 24 and 31 fps on an AGA machine with a 68030/50.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Robinson's Requiem Enhanced

Robinson's Requiem Enhanced, a major overhaul of the unforgiving 1994 classic that requires WHDLoad 20 or newer and 1 MB of Fast memory. This latest release tackles several long-standing technical quirks of the original game, finally squashing a notorious audio bug where sound effects would abruptly cut out to a simple click after playing just once. AGA users running certain 68040 setups will also be relieved to find that the intro sequences and menus are no longer skewed, while a new movement speed option (Custom1) lets players choose between walking at the classic ECS 1X pace or the brisker AGA 2X speed.

The real star of the show, however, is the dramatic visual and performance upgrade delivered to the game's 3D world. Enabled by default in the installed icon, the new enhanced framerate option (Custom2=1) delivers a noticeably faster and smoother 3D view, especially on systems utilizing Fast memory above 16 MB—such as Zorro III or most 68040 and 68060 accelerator boards—which the game now taps into for a serious speed boost. To top it off, AGA players get the added bonus of a smooth landscape feature (Custom3=1, also active by default), ensuring that distant hills keep their proper shape rather than warping as you turn around to survey the alien wilderness.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Virus Enhanced


Virus Enhanced, a brand-new overhaul that brings modern fluidity and stability to the iconic title. Built to play nicely across the entire Amiga hardware line up, the update ensures the title screen no longer flashes by in an instant on accelerated machines, while the attract screen no longer drags on slower setups. Under the hood, Vesuri also resolved compatibility quirks on newer processors by flushing the instruction cache whenever the game modifies its own code, and added a handy mouse sensitivity option (CUSTOM3) allowing pilots to dial controls in at 100%, 75%, 50%, or 25%.


Performance gets a massive boost too thanks to the new enhanced framerate feature (CUSTOM1, switched on by default in the installed icon), which decouples pacing from hardware quirks so the game runs at a consistent speed on every Amiga—with CUSTOM2 letting players pick their preferred pace. Better yet, if your machine is equipped with FastMem, the game now runs and draws directly inside it, unlocking silky-smooth visuals at up to 50 frames per second by interpolating motion between the game's original logic steps.


▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Star Wars Enhanced


And the last write up is for Star Wars Enhanced! This update keeps the timing fix permanently switched on—repurposing CUSTOM2 (enabled by default in the installed icon) into a new "Enhanced framerate" mode that interpolates the gameplay, attract scenes, and wave select screen at up to 50 frames per second at the game's original speed on an A1200 with fast RAM or a faster CPU (using SPS 403), while stock A500 and A1200 setups draw just as before. Alongside the smoother visuals, Vesuri squashed a host of classic bugs: 68060 users no longer lose words or strokes in the vector text on the wave select and scoring screens, the wave select menu no longer races ahead on fast CPUs or suffers from a black box cutting into the WAVE 1 text and Death Star, and space finally returns to pitch black instead of staying grey or tinted after taking hits and screen flashes.

entry.title: Flashback 25th Anniversary Edition repainted for AGA/RTG 1.0 by AmiKit
entry.content:
Conrad B. Hart has made his return to his original home on the Commodore Amiga, courtesy of a massive new release from AmiKIT. While the legendary cinematic platformer first debuted on the Amiga back in 1992 before jumping to PCs and consoles, this newly announced port of Flashback: 25th Anniversary Edition brings the game full circle. Decades after the original release, fans can experience the classic sci-fi adventure once again, only this time it arrives with a complete audio visual overhaul that outshines even the 2018 PC remaster.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Available in three distinct versions for different hardware setups, the port scales from a standard Amiga 1200 running in 640x256 AGA all the way up to 1024x896 RTG for machines equipped with a graphics card. Using a custom converter that pulls assets from your own copy of the game, the port trades the look of the original Amiga 500 release for smoothed or fully repainted high-definition visuals. On RTG systems, cutscenes run at up to four times the original resolution, moving objects are smoothed in real time, and the audio gets a major boost with remastered music and panoramic stereo sound effects—an upgrade missing from the 2018 PC version.

What truly sets this AmiKIT release apart is how it solves the biggest complaint aimed at the modern PC remaster. Rather than simply stretching and blurring the old 1993 256x224 artwork, AmiKIT’s converter runs every background through the ArtStation neural model to transform dithered pixels into crisp, painted HD textures. Character animations for both Conrad and his enemies also get a major facelift on RTG setups using the BigFArt model, replacing rigid pixels with clean, modern artwork. With its sharp repainted graphics and immersive stereo audio, this may give Amiga owners another reason to step back in the world of Flashback.

entry.title: Shadow of the Beast 3 - The trilogy is now complete on the Mega Drive!
entry.content:
While Sega Mega Drive owners got to experience the first two Shadow of the Beast games back in the 16-bit era, the third and final chapter famously never made the jump to the console. Now, more than thirty years later, a solo developer known as juicelink has finally fixed that missing piece with an unofficial conversion of Shadow of the Beast III. Rather than relying on an Amiga emulator, this latest recreation runs natively on actual Mega Drive hardware, bringing the missing piece of the iconic trilogy to Sega’s machine at last.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

According to the developer via their itch io page, what originally started out as a small proof-of-concept demo featuring just the opening forest level, its enemies, and a boss fight has now grown into a full release. Juicelink recently confirmed that the entire game has been converted and can be played all the way through to the end—a massive undertaking that the developer noted was built with some assistance from Claude. While it isn't a long-lost official port, it faithfully captures the spirit of the Amiga original while finally completing the trilogy for both Sega and Shadow of the Beast fans alike.

And that's not all, juicelink also took the opportunity to smooth out some of the original release's notorious rough edges. Anyone who played the 1992 Amiga version remembers how easy it was to get hopelessly lost, so this Mega Drive conversion adds a handy notification system to alert players when a puzzle hasn't been solved yet, alongside an option to restart from checkpoints. Though a few minor bugs may still be lurking, the full game is ready to play, and the developer is actively welcoming feedback from the retro gaming community.

entry.title: Lands of Lore AGA - Westwood's incredible PC Dungeon Crawler could be coming to the Amiga!
entry.content:
After more than six years of blood, sweat, and tears, developer Vairn has revealed a native Commodore Amiga port of Westwood Studios' classic dungeon crawler, Lands of Lore is in the works. Prompted into the final stretch after seeing fellow coder Cfou experiment with an AI-assisted port, Vairn is building Lands of Lore AGA entirely with hand-rolled C code—zero AI and zero chunky-to-planar (C2P) routines involved. Powered by the Amiga C Engine (ACE), which actually gained AGA chipset support specifically because of this project, the port converts the original PC chunky graphics, MT-32 tracks, and audio into Amiga Blitter-friendly assets, MODs, and 8SVX files. While Vairn initially got a stripped-down version running on a base machine without Fast RAM, the sheer volume of monster animations, multi-textured wallsets, and extra colours far surpasses games like Eye of the Beholder, making an 020 Amiga 1200 with 4MB of Fast RAM a firm requirement.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Lands of Lore AGA - Vairn

Although the game is already playable, Vairn notes that a few finishing touches are still needed before release, including squashing some graphical bugs, polishing the music, and wrapping up the spell system. Currently, the heavy lifting of asset conversion is handled externally via Python scripts on PC, Mac, or Linux—which crunch the data roughly 10,000 times faster than native hardware—though a standalone Amiga conversion executable is planned for the future. Even with a bit of polish left to go, Lands of Lore AGA is shaping up to be an impressive labour of love for classic Amiga RPG fans.

Links :1) Source 

Lands Of Lore AGA (EOB2 AGA update) - CFou!

In parallel to Vairn’s hand-rolled effort, veteran Amiga coder CFou!—known for his previous AGA ports of Eye of the Beholder I & II and Dune II—is also tackling a port of Lands of Lore, though he has turned to artificial intelligence to help cross the finish line on a goal he first set back in 2006. After hitting a wall with the game's complex EMC2 scripts, CFou! decided to test AI tools like Claude and Fable 5.2 to build a brand-new assembly engine from scratch, using the AI to reverse-engineer internal game logic, generate format documentation, adapt music, and build extraction tools. The resulting build already features working intros, endings, level exploration, fog, shadows, and even CD voice support via .TLK files. Yet, despite the impressive technical progress, CFou! admits the experience feels bittersweet; while he is astounded by what the AI can accomplish, he laments that his own coding skills feel increasingly obsolete, leaving him feeling more like a beta-tester than a programmer on what will likely be his final Amiga project.

entry.title: Race or Destroy - A fast top-down Amiga AGA racing game for 1 to 3 players via AI/qupe75
entry.content:
Sitting at home with a bunch of friends round for a drink then developer qupe75 might have you covered with his latest release for the Commodore Amiga called Race or Destroy. Drawing heavy inspiration from retro favorites like Super Sprint, Super Cars, and Off Road Racer, this fast-paced, single-screen top-down racer lets one to three players battle it out on the same machine using a mix of joysticks and the keyboard. You can stick to standard weapon-assisted laps, crank up the carnage in the "Race or Destroy" mode where pickups can completely wreck your rivals, or ditch the tracks altogether for last-car-standing brawls across five Destruction Derby arenas complete with sudden death overtime.


Beyond quick single races and time trials, the game has further replay value with six full championship cups—ranging from Warm Up to Ultimate—plus a custom "Own Cup" creator that supports up to eight racers at once and 20 saveable achievements. Even getting blown up doesn't mean the action stops: while a rescue helicopter hauls smashed vehicles off the asphalt, surviving drivers have to sprint for a safe zone on foot. That creates a frantic mini-game where you're desperately trying to escape on foot while rivals swerve to run you down for a bonus championship point.


Requirements

  • An AGA Amiga (A1200, A4000 or CD32 with a keyboard), PAL.
  • 2 MB chip RAM and at least 4 MB fast RAM. It uses nearly all of a stock A1200's chip RAM, so close other programs first. 8 MB fast is comfortable.
  • A hard disk. The game saves a small file in its own drawer.
  • It runs from Workbench or a Shell. It is not a WHDLoad install.

Race or Destroy was a personal feature request by the developer

entry.title: Cyclone CPC - 1984 Speccy game gets an Amstrad 128k port via NBSystems
entry.content:
ZX Spectrum Version

Forty plus years after its original 1984 debut on the ZX Spectrum, the classic helicopter rescue-em-up Cyclone has unofficially landed on the Amstrad CPC 128K thanks to developer NBSystems. Originally coded by Vortex Software co-founder Costa Panayi as a sequel to Tornado Low Level, this multidirectional action title famously skipped the CPC during the 8-bit heyday. NBSystems has stepped in to right that historical wrong, giving Amstrad owners a dedicated port packed with CPC visuals, new graphics, smoother movement, and an original soundtrack.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Amstrad CPC Version

In Cyclone CPC, players take the controls of a rescue helicopter tasked with scouring a sprawling archipelago of 14 islands to recover five crates of vital medical supplies. The catch is that a deadly, roaming cyclone threatens to tear your chopper apart at any moment, forcing pilots to balance careful navigation with urgent rescue runs. With its faithful gameplay loop and modernised Amstrad presentation, this long-overdue conversion offers CPC owners a fresh excuse to fire up their machines and check out this classic 1980's game originally by Vortex Software.
